summary.text: A previously healthy 13-year-old presented with a 3-day history of abdominal pain, nausea and emesis. He was found to have fulminant hepatic failure and was listed for liver transplantation. Over the next 24 hours he was transferred to the intensive care unit, intubated and started on molecular adsorbent recirculating system treatment. He had right upper quadrant tenderness with palpable hepatomegaly.

Total bilirubin was 8.0 mg/dL and INR 8.0, consistent with acute liver failure. Abdominal ultrasound showed a heterogenous and coarsened appearance of hepatic parenchyma. The explanted liver later showed diffuse acute lobular injury with cholestasis and mixed inflammation. His family history included a non-specified autoimmune disease in his paternal grandmother.

He received a liver transplant using a liver from a 25 year-old female donor who died of anoxia secondary to drug intoxication, preserved with normothermic machine perfusion, performed with the piggyback technique. The liver reperfused well and functioned immediately; transaminases began decreasing within 24 hours, bilirubin and INR were normal by post-operative day 4, and he was discharged home on post-operative day 7. No post-reperfusion syndrome or early allograft dysfunction occurred.

One moderate to severe acute cellular rejection occurred 24 months after transplant and was treated with pulse-dosed steroids. He has had no other readmissions, is doing well with normal liver function and has returned to activities such as soccer; the stated follow-up of 28 months conflicts with the abstract range of 7 to 16 months.

summary.text: An 8-year-old male had liver cirrhosis from Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis Type 3 with portal hypertension, atopic dermatitis and dental caries, and was listed for liver transplantation at 4 years of age. His brother has cirrhosis from the same condition and two uncles have an unspecified liver disease. Examination showed hepatosplenomegaly.

Alkaline phosphatase was 510 units/L (elevated), aspartate transaminase 78 units/L, alanine transaminase 52 units/L, total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL and INR normal at 1.0. CT showed a nodular liver contour, massive splenomegaly and gastric and esophageal varices, and the explanted liver showed cirrhosis and cholestasis.

The donor liver, from a 7-year-old donor, was preserved with normothermic machine perfusion because of logistical timing issues, with arterial cannulation via the thoracic aorta and portal cannulation after an interposition graft. The recipient surgery used the piggyback fashion and the liver functioned immediately. Transaminases fell from 12 hours, bilirubin and INR normalized by 72 hours, and he was discharged on post-operative day 12.

The abstract states all patients are currently doing well and that no recipient had post-reperfusion syndrome or early allograft dysfunction. An unlabeled follow-up paragraph describing 17 months post-transplant with normal liver function, no readmissions and full return to school is only tentatively mapped to this patient and is quarantined for review.

summary.text: A 19-year-old female with hypoplastic left heart syndrome status post Fontan procedure with revision developed Fontan associated liver disease with cirrhosis and had a history of gastritis. She was referred to a pediatric hospital before age 18 for combined heart and liver transplant evaluation and was listed for combined heart-liver transplantation. She had no abnormal examination findings and normal size for age.

Laboratory work-up showed no significant abnormalities, with mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase of 162 units/L, INR 1.1 and total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL. Pre-transplant abdominal MRI showed cirrhosis, splenomegaly and a splenorenal shunt, and the explanted liver was consistent with Fontan associated liver disease with grade 3 fibrosis.

The donor was a 22-year-old male who died of head trauma; liver and heart were procured and placed on OCS devices, with NMP of the liver used because of the prolonged wait to finish the heart transplant. The liver was transplanted sequentially after the heart in the bicaval fashion, with 13 hours 31 minutes from cross clamp to implant. Transaminases, bilirubin and INR peaked early then fell.

On post-operative day seven she returned to the operating room for abdominal washout of a hematoma, attributed to heparin anticoagulation during hemofiltration; allograft function was maintained, renal recovery occurred and she was discharged on day 34. She was readmitted one month post-transplant for a biliary anastomotic stricture treated with ERCP, sphincterotomy and stent placement, since resolved, and is doing well.
